ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The SISSA Ethics Committee approved the present study with protocol number 8401-III/13.
All procedures, including inclusion/exclusion criteria, informed consent procedures, ethical approval, and compensation, were identical to Experiment 1.

Participants were exposed to visual streams of either structured or randomly organized linguistic stimuli (i.e., words and pseudofonts) while performing a demanding visual 3-back matching task on the color of a central fixation cross.
A total of 44 participants took part in the experiment.

All participants were right-handed native Italian speakers, aged between 18 and 35 years, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of linguistic, cognitive, or neurological impairment.
Participants provided their written informed consent before starting the experiment and were kept unaware of the experiment's hypotheses until the end of the session.
both the structured and random conditions, participants were exposed to eight visual streams (i.e., trials) of 1080 stimuli presented in sequential order.
Arbitrarily, we defined one set as the "base" set and one set as the "oddball" set, and we arranged the Participants were concurrently asked to perform a demanding visual 3back, color-matching task.
Participants were instructed to perform a 3-back task in which they had to press a key ("m") when the current color of the cross was the same as 3 changes prior.
Participants were informed that they would see a stream of words or symbols (i.e., pseudofonts) in the background, but were asked to ignore them and focus on the cross color instead.

To collect enough data points within each trial and to ensure participants were sufficiently engaged, we imposed a constraint that required the 3-back match to occur at least 15 times out of the total 30 color changes during each trial.
Random intercepts for participants were included in all models.
Random intercepts for participants were included in all models, and the selected model also featured a random slope for conditions within participants.
In a within-subjects design, participants completed a 3-back, color-matching task while viewing either a random stream or a structured stream.
A total of 42 participants took part in the experiment.

One participant had a mean RT of 6.29 s in the low-load condition (group median = 0.49 s; maximum among the remaining participants = 0.90 s), and the other had a mean RT of 6.37 s in the high-load condition (group median = 0.94 s; maximum = 2.12 s).
During the low-load condition, participants were instructed to perform a color-change detection task (i.e., press the 'm' key on the keyboard whenever the central fixation cross changed color).
These results indicate that participants were attentive and proficient in completing both tasks, performing significantly above chance levels.

Participants showed robust neural entrainment at the frequency of the embedded structure, indicating that their online sensitivity to structure persists even when participants are challenged with a competing, attention-demanding task.
Behavioral results confirmed the effectiveness of the manipulation: participants were clearly slower and less accurate in the high-load condition than in the low-load condition.

The main logic of the experiment rests on the fact that, if participants are sensitive to this frequency difference, we should observe neural entrainment at the presentation frequency of the oddballs (1.2 Hz), which would indicate online sensitivity to the frequency-based structure.
Participants completed eight trials per condition (16 trials in total: 2 conditions × 2 stimulus types × 4 repetitions), presented in random order within each condition.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The human brain readily captures regularities in the environment.
It is not clear, however, whether and how this skill-statistical learninginteracts with attention.
We addressed this issue by leveraging neural entrainment, the synchronization of brain activity with statistical structure.

In Study 1, we asked whether sensitivity to a frequencybased regularity, created by embedding low-frequency items among higher-frequency items, competes for attentional resources with a concurrent task.
Participants viewed structured or random visual streams while performing a 3-back color matching task.
Neural entrainment emerged only for structured streams, demonstrating sensitivity to the frequency structure.

Improvement in the concurrent task, indexed by decreasing response times, unfolded more slowly when structure was present, suggesting that detecting statistical regularities drew attention away from the 3-back color matching task.
In Study 2, we tested the reverse connection-whether taxing attention with a more difficult task impairs the neural tracking of statistical structure.
We compared entrainment during an easier color-change detection task and a more difficult 3-back color matching task.
We observed no detectable effect of attentional load on neural entrainment.

These findings reveal an asymmetric relationship between attention and frequency-based statistical learning: detecting structure imposes a modest attentional cost on a concurrent behavioral task, whereas the online neural tracking of regularities appears to be unaffected by increased attentional demands.
Our sensory world is extremely complex.
At any given moment, we are hit by a multiplicity of sights, sounds, and movements that form a tangled web of cues and signals.
Interpreting this complexity is very challenging.
Yet, our brain detects recurring patterns in the environment, often without our conscious awareness-a capacity known as statistical learning.
Although interest in statistical learning dates back nearly a century (Frost et al., 2019), it surged following demonstrations of its fundamental role in language acquisition (Saffran et al., 1996).

text.text: Since then, statistical learning has been observed across sensory modalities (Conway & Christiansen, 2005; Frost et al., 2015), stages of development (Forest et al., 2023), and even across species (Conway & Christiansen, 2001; Santolin & Saffran, 2018), establishing it as a pervasive mechanism through which the brain extracts and represents structure in the environment (Sherman et al., 2020).

text.text: Far less is known about whether (and, if so, how) regularities are prioritized for processing amid the vast array of competing environmental information.

text.text: Answering this question requires considering the relationship between statistical learning on the one hand, and attention and cognitive load on the other.
Quite interestingly, the interaction between attention and statistical learning can be examined from two complementary perspectives.
First, structured input may influence how we allocate our attention by allowing statistical regularities to prioritize certain aspects of the environment over others.

Indeed, statistical regularities can bias selective attention toward predictable targets and away from distractors (Ferrante et al., 2018; Geng & Behrmann, 2002 , 2005; Jiang et al., 2013; Wang & Theeuwes, 2018).

text.text: Accumulating evi-dence also suggests that the mere presence of statistical regularities attracts attention (Forest et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2013) and stabilizes moment-tomoment attentional states (Greatti et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Accumulating evi-dence also suggests that the mere presence of statistical regularities attracts attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Forest et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Zhao et al., 2013)</ref> and stabilizes moment-tomoment attentional states <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Greatti et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To date, however, it remains unknown whether this attentional attraction persists when statistical regularities compete with an ongoing task for attentional resources.

If the processing of statistical structure competes for limited attentional resources, then task-irrelevant regularities should draw resources away from a concurrent task, resulting in measurable costs to task performance.

Testing this possibility requires paradigms in which structured input and a concurrent task compete for attention while remaining otherwise independent, allowing the attentional cost of statistical learning, if any, to emerge.
Second, the availability of attentional resources may determine the extent to which statistical regularities are detected and learned.

Research on both auditory and visual statistical learning has produced inconsistent evidence about whether learning requires attention or can occur automatically: some studies suggest that attention facilitates statistical learning (D. text.text: Yet, these sequential dependencies represent only one form of statistical structure available in the environment.
Regularities can also arise from differences in the frequency with which individual events occur, for example.

Such frequency information can provide an important source of structure, contributing, for instance, to the discovery of grammatical categories during language learning (Mintz, 2003; Reeder et al., 2013).

text.text: Yet, whether the interaction between attention and statistical learning generalizes beyond sequential dependencies to frequency-based structure remains unknown.
In the present work, we address these open issues in the literature through neural entrainment-the brain's synchronization with statistical structure.

This approach offers an online, objective measure of neural sensitivity that allows researchers to observe whether the participants' brains are capturing structure during exposure, in the absence of any behavioral assessment. Indeed, in De Rosa et al. (2022), participants viewed rapid sequences of base elements presented at a high frequency (F).

text.text: Oddball stimuli were inserted at fixed intervals (every n items), thus creating a second regularity (periodic at F/n) based on the appearance of a lower frequency item.

Importantly, the higher and lower frequency items were of the same sort (e.g., words in words), thus making their relative frequency of occurrence within the stream the only possible cue to the presence of a statistical structure.
Indeed, EEG data revealed neural entrainment at F/n, indicating implicit discrimination between the higher-and lower-frequency groups.
These findings broadened the scope of entrainment to statistical structure beyond TPs.

Although this emerging evidence demonstrates that the brain can reliably track frequencybased statistical structure online, very little is known, again, about how this process interacts with attention.

This interaction may operate in both directions also for univariate cues, of course: frequency-based structure may draw attention away from competing tasks, while the availability of attentional resources may constrain the neural processing of such structure.

The present study addresses the relationship between statistical learning and attention, combining attentional (cognitive workload) manipulations with neural entrainment as an online index of learning.
Study 1 manipulates the presence vs. absence of statistical structure and checks whether this yields effects on performance in a concurrent task.

Participants were exposed to visual streams of either structured or randomly organized linguistic stimuli (i.e., words and pseudofonts) while performing a demanding visual 3-back matching task on the color of a central fixation cross.
If statistical regularities attract attention, we predict that performance on the 3-back task will be impaired during structured streams compared to random streams.

Alternatively, no difference in performance between conditions would suggest that the detection of frequency-based regularities does not affect attention, at least to the extent that this can be captured in a concurrent behavioral task.
Study 2 manipulates attentional demands to determine whether they influence the neural processing of statistical structure.

Participants viewed the same structured visual streams from Study 1 while performing either a high-load (3-back matching) or low-load (mere detection) concurrent task on the color of a cross superimposed on the stream.
This within-subject design allows us to isolate the effect of attentional demands on the neural representation of statistical structure.

The cross changed color 30 times per trial, alternating between red (RGB: 255, 0, 0), blue (RGB: 0, 0, 255), and light green (RGB: 0, 204, 0).

Participants were instructed to perform a 3-back task in which they had to press a key ("m") when the current color of the cross was the same as 3 changes prior.
Participants were informed that they would see a stream of words or symbols (i.e., pseudofonts) in the background, but were asked to ignore them and focus on the cross color instead.
Instructions were provided in written form, and the experimenter ensured that participants fully understood the task before initiating the experiment.

To collect enough data points within each trial and to ensure participants were sufficiently engaged, we imposed a constraint that required the 3-back match to occur at least 15 times out of the total 30 color changes during each trial.

In Study 1, we examined whether the mere presence of a statistical pattern reduces the attentional resources available to perform a concurrent task.
In a within-subjects design, participants completed a 3-back, color-matching task while viewing either a random stream or a structured stream.
We hypothesized that if statistical regularities compete for attentional resources, concurrent task performance would be impaired when such regularities are present.

As expected, robust neural entrainment at the oddball frequency (1.2 Hz) emerged only in the structured condition and for both words and pseudofonts, replicating De Rosa et al. ( 2022) and confirming that participants successfully tracked the embedded structure.

text.text: This validates the effectiveness of our manipulation: neural sensitivity to structure appeared exclusively when the said structure was present.

Behaviorally, no main effect of condition was observed on the 3-back task performance, either in terms of accuracy or overall RTs, indicating that the presence of statistical regularities did not directly disrupt participants' ability to perform the concurrent task.

However, we observed a significant interaction between condition and trial number for RTs: although participants became faster over the course of the study in both conditions, the rate of their improvement was slower in the structured condition, where a statistical pattern was embedded.

Overall, these findings demonstrate that the brain is remarkably sensitive to frequency-based structure, detecting such regularities even while attention is engaged by a cognitively demanding concurrent task.
However, processing this structure did not consume sufficient resources to impair overall task accuracy or response speed.

Instead, the regularities imposed a subtler attentional cost: although participants successfully performed the concurrent task, their practice-related improvements in response speed unfolded more slowly in the presence of structured input.
Thus, frequency-based regularities appear to compete modestly for attention without substantially disrupting ongoing performance.

text.text: Together, these results support the view that statistical learning of frequencybased structures may be robust to attentional manipulation, at least as measured via neural entrainment.
In two experiments, we examined the relationship between attention and the neural sensitivity to frequency-based statistical structure.

In Study 1, we manipulated the presence of task-irrelevant visual regularities during a demanding 3-back, color-matching task to test whether processing statistical structure imposes a measurable cost on concurrent behavior.

Participants showed robust neural entrainment at the frequency of the embedded structure, indicating that their online sensitivity to structure persists even when participants are challenged with a competing, attention-demanding task.

Behaviorally, we found no measurable difference in the 3-back, colormatching accuracy and mean RTs when frequency-based regularities were present, suggesting that the presence of a frequency-based structure does not disrupt participants' ability to perform the concurrent task.
Yet, improvements in task performance, as indexed by decreasing RTs across trials, unfolded more slowly when regularities were present than when the stream was random.

This finding suggests that attention and statistical learning may not be fully independent: the presence of a structured stream might have attracted attention (or cognitive resources more generally) away from the concurrent task, reducing the rate at which performance improved with practice.

Note that the structured input was entirely task-irrelevant, and our instructions even encouraged participants to ignore it; thus, our findings are consistent with the idea that our attentional system is automatically attracted toward structure once regularities are detected in the environment, in line with previous work (Greatti et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2013).

text.text: The effect is, however, rather mild; it affects the speed of learning and improvement, not performance per se.

Therefore, the presence of frequency regularities in the input might behave as a mild attentional pull, drawing enough resources to flag the presence of learnable structure, but leaving sufficient capacity for successfully completing other concurrent tasks.

This balance is likely adaptive: because regularities are ubiquitous in natural environments, their detection must remain sufficiently sensitive to support learning without compromising the goal-directed behaviors in which we are concurrently engaged.

In Study 2, we reversed the causal question: rather than asking whether statistical regularities capture attention, we tested whether taxing attention with a more difficult concurrent task constrains the online neural sensitivity to frequency-based structure.
Participants viewed the same structured visual streams as in Study 1 while performing either a low-load (color detection) or high-load (3-back color matching) task.
This design allowed us to manipulate cognitive load and, consequently, the attentional resources available to process statistical structure.
Behavioral results confirmed the effectiveness of the manipulation: participants were clearly slower and less accurate in the high-load condition than in the low-load condition.

Yet, neural entrainment at the oddball frequency (1.2 Hz) did not differ between conditions, suggesting that our neural sensitivity to statistical regularities may operate independently of the cognitive load imposed by a competing task.
This dissociation suggests that the mechanisms supporting online statistical learning are resource-tolerant; they can extract and integrate regularities even when attention is engaged elsewhere.
These findings are nicely in line with previous work on the relationship between attention and statistical learning.
For example, Batterink and Paller (2019) also showed that entrainment to regularities is unaffected by the manipulation of attention through a concurrent task.

text.text: Our work, however, extends the theoretical remit of Batterink and Paller's results in at least two important ways.

First, the regularity implemented in our stream of stimuli was based on a frequency difference between groups of items (A and B occur more often, C and D occur more rarely), rather than on TPs, that is, predictive relationships between individual stimuli (A predicts B, C predicts D).
These forms of structure place different computational demands on learners.

Frequency learning requires accumulating evidence across relatively extended periods to estimate how often individual events occur, whereas TP learning depends on detecting local relationships between successive events.

However, frequency statistics are representationally less complex because they concern individual items rather than the associations between them; they are based on univariate, rather than multivariate information.
The two forms of regularity also afford predictions at different levels of specificity.

In frequency-based streams, learners could anticipate whether the next stimulus was likely to belong to the frequent or infrequent category (i.e., bases or oddballs), but could not predict the identity of the particular stimulus.
In TP-based structures, by contrast, the occurrence of one element constrains which specific element is likely to follow, enabling item-level predictions.

As previously proposed (Greatti et al., 2026), these statistics may therefore serve complementary computational functions, with frequency information providing a coarse representation of the distributional properties of the environment, and TP-based information supporting more precise models of its sequential organization.

text.text: Despite this methodological shift, the convergence of our findings closely parallels results obtained with TP-based statistics.

The persistence of neural entrainment under these conditions suggests that statistical learning, at least as measured through its early neural index, may rely on a common mechanism that generalizes across different forms of structure (Growns et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The persistence of neural entrainment under these conditions suggests that statistical learning, at least as measured through its early neural index, may rely on a common mechanism that generalizes across different forms of structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Growns et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A second way in which the present work extends our knowledge on the relationship between attention and statistical learning is in the role of the perceptual channel.
Prior research focused on acoustic statistical learning (see, e.g., Batterink and Paller, 2019), while we assess learning in the visual domain.

Our results suggest that, at least in the present paradigm, vision and audition share a common learning mechanism -or at least they feature mechanisms that are similarly independent of attention and cognitive load.

Moreover, learning occurred here in the same perceptual modality as the competing task, while in previous work the attentional manipulation was deployed cross-modally (e.g., statistical regularities were implemented in the acoustic modality while the concurrent task was visual).

Because attentional interference is typically stronger within than between modalities (J. Duncan et al., 1997; Soto-Faraco & Spence, 2002; Treisman & Davies, 1973; Wickens et al., 1984), this finding provides a particularly conservative test of the robustness of statistical learning under reduced attention, and it indicates that the lack of an attentional load effect on neural entrainment cannot simply be attributed to cross-modal resource segregation; rather, it appears to reflect a genuinely resource-tolerant mechanism of perceptual statistical learning.

text.text: It is important to note that our findings do not imply that learning, in the traditional sense of storing and retrieving information to guide behavior, is independent of attention.
Our measure of learning (i.e., neural entrainment to statistical regularities) indexes the online perceptual tracking of structure rather than its encoding.

While frequency tagging provides a precise and bias-free index of perceptual sensitivity to regularities, it remains unclear whether such entrainment translates into explicit or behaviorally usable knowledge (Ruzza & Crepaldi, 2026).
text.formatted: While frequency tagging provides a precise and bias-free index of perceptual sensitivity to regularities, it remains unclear whether such entrainment translates into explicit or behaviorally usable knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ruzza & Crepaldi, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These considerations are in line with the view that the online component of statistical learning (i.e., neural entrainment) is dissociable from the memory storage or retrieval component of statistical learning (as measured by offline statistical learning tasks).
Indeed, prior work has often reported weak or absent correlations between neural entrainment and behavioral measures (Batterink et al., 2024; Smalle et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Indeed, prior work has often reported weak or absent correlations between neural entrainment and behavioral measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Batterink et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Smalle et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, our results should be interpreted as evidence that the early perceptual registration of structure seems to be robust to attentional load, not that the memory encoding of these regularities is attention-independent.

The transition from perceptual detection to stable memory representations goes beyond the purpose of our study and may still critically depend on attentional engagement (e.g., Turk-Browne et al., 2005).
text.formatted: The transition from perceptual detection to stable memory representations goes beyond the purpose of our study and may still critically depend on attentional engagement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Turk-Browne et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, it is worth noting a secondary finding, which, however, reveals another interesting aspect of the relationship between statistical learning and attention.
Both Study 1 and Study 2 showed stronger neural entrainment at the structure frequency (1.2 Hz) for words than for pseudofonts.
Interestingly, this neural enhancement did not translate into greater interference with the concurrent task: accuracy and RTs did not differ between word and pseudofont trials in either study.

The word advantage may reflect facilitation from pre-existing orthographic and lexical representations, which could support more precise predictions and thereby enhance neural sensitivity to frequency-based structure.
Future research should build on this possibility to determine whether -and if so, under which conditions -different item categories modulate neural sensitivity to statistical regularities.
Overall, our results offer a general view of statistical learning and attention as interdependent, but separable systems.

Statistical learning appears to operate through an automatic, resource-tolerant perceptual mechanism that flexibly interacts with attention: it attracts it when structure is present, and it persists even when attentional resources are limited.

More generally, this pattern suggests that the brain continuously tracks statistical structure through low-level mechanisms of sensory synchronization, while higher-level attentional processes might still determine whether that structure becomes encoded into memory or guides behavior.
